newsitem.title: INDIA: Airfreight City for Delhi - to build or not to build?
newsitem.headline: Airfreight City for Delhi - to build or not to build?

text.p: NEW DELHI, March 19, Reuter - Plans for an "Airfreight City" located near Delhi could now be unnecessary due to dramatic improvements in export cargo handling, industry sources said.
The development, near Gurgaon next to the New Delhi Indira Gandhi International airport, was first mooted three years ago.

Export cargo handling at the four main international airports (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennal and Calcutta) has seen marked improvement, with waiting times reduced significantly, Airports Authority of India (AAI) sources said.
Expanding infrastructure facilities and freedom of operation for the private air cargo (PAC) industry sector have been the focus of internal debate in the industry for some time, they added.

The Airport City cargo hub plan was put forward by the Indian Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO) to the last Congress government for cabinet approval. However general elections last year brought in a new government, and the proposal has had to rejoin the approval queue again.
ITPO officials said they are now seeking approval to undertake a feasibility study, not to actually start building the facility.

One concept is that the new 'Airfreight City' should be modelled on Changi in Singapore. The ITPO and the AAI would act as developers, not financiers, for the 200 acre site, which would also work as a transfer hub for the region's South Asian Association of Regional Cooperation (SAARC) countries.
The AAI recently suggested that it would need an investment of some $75m to upgrade its cargo facilities around the country's airports over the next few years.
The average waiting for cargo handling in January 1996 was five days but by January this year it had fallen to 2.2 days for 98 percent of cargo, the remainder being moved on the third day.
However they added that the dwell time for import cargo has increased from an average stay time of 21 days to 30 days in the 12 months to January 1997.
AAI sources added they have been considering an increase in storage charges and reducing the free dwell time to two days from seven days in 1998.
This would be to pressure importers to stop using the four main cargo terminals as cheap warehousing.

They said it would be possible to free up substantial storage capacity if they got the average import dwell time down to five days from its present 30 days. This would also reduce the need for the proposed $75m investment in cargo terminals, they said. -- Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
